quote: You are fellow citizens with the holy ones.
firstReading: Paul proclaims that those once far off are now members of God’s household. The Church is not merely a gathering of separate believers: it is a holy structure built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets. Christ Jesus is the indispensable cornerstone, holding the whole building together and causing it to grow into a sacred temple. In him, believers are being built into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.
psalmSummary: Psalm 19 celebrates the universal witness of creation. The heavens recount God’s glory, and the firmament makes known the work of his hands. Day and night continually communicate this praise without ordinary human speech, yet their proclamation reaches throughout the earth. On the feast of apostles, this cosmic hymn complements the Church’s mission: God’s saving truth is to be announced among all peoples.
gospelSummary: Luke recounts that Jesus goes out to the mountain and spends the night in prayer to God before choosing the Twelve. At daybreak, he calls his disciples and appoints twelve of them as apostles, giving them a distinct share in his mission. The list includes Simon Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Simon called the Zealot, Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot. Simon and Jude belong to this prayerfully chosen apostolic body. Their place in the list underscores that their dignity rests first on Christ’s call, not on extensive recorded accomplishments. The Gospel also shows that apostolic ministry arises from Jesus’ communion with the Father and remains ordered to his saving purpose.
saintReflection: Saints Simon and Jude, Apostles (Feast): The Feast of Saints Simon and Jude honors two apostles named in the Gospel lists among the Twelve chosen by Jesus. Simon is called the Zealot, while Jude is distinguished from Judas Iscariot and is traditionally associated with the Letter of Jude. Scripture provides few biographical details, and later missionary traditions differ, but their apostolic identity is the foundation of the feast. They were called into communion with Christ, formed by his teaching, and sent to bear witness to the Kingdom. The diversity within the Twelve shows Jesus creating a new people whose unity comes from his call rather than identical backgrounds. Ephesians describes the Church as built upon the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ as cornerstone. Simon and Jude invite fidelity to apostolic teaching, persevering prayer, missionary courage, and unity centered upon the Lord.
dailyPrayer:
Lord Jesus Christ, before choosing the Twelve, you remained in prayer with the Father. Draw your Church into that same prayerful communion, so that every word of witness may arise from listening to you. On this feast of Saints Simon and Jude, we thank you for the apostles upon whose foundation you have built your holy people.

Make us steadfast in the teaching handed down through the apostles. Guard us from division, confusion, and self-will, and root us ever more deeply in you, the cornerstone. As you gathered disciples of differing backgrounds into one apostolic company, gather your people in the unity of faith, hope, and charity.

Grant us the courage to confess your Kingdom with humility and perseverance. May the witness of Simon and Jude teach us to value the hidden fidelity of those who belong wholly to you. Let the praise proclaimed by the heavens awaken our hearts to adore you, and make our lives a faithful proclamation of your mercy. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
The readings present the apostolic Church as the work of the Triune God. Jesus prays to the Father and appoints the Twelve, revealing that apostolic mission begins in the Son’s communion with the Father. The Spirit, according to Ephesians, makes the baptized into God’s dwelling place. The Church is therefore holy not because her members are self-sufficient, but because Christ gathers, sustains, and inhabits her.

Simon and Jude belong to the apostolic foundation named by Paul. Their feast directs attention beyond the limited details preserved about their lives to the grace of their calling and the enduring authority of apostolic witness. Christ remains the cornerstone: the apostles do not replace him, but serve his definitive revelation and transmit the faith received from him.

Psalm 19 broadens this vision. Creation declares God’s glory everywhere, while the apostolic preaching carries the saving Gospel to the nations. The Church’s unity is not sameness of origin or temperament. It is communion in Christ, fidelity to the apostolic faith, and life in the Holy Spirit.
exegesis:
Context: The feast joins two apostles whose names appear among the Twelve chosen by Jesus. Luke’s account is notably restrained. It does not recount individual deeds of Simon the Zealot or Judas son of James, traditionally called Jude; it situates them within the body of apostles appointed by the Lord. This reserve is itself instructive. Their ecclesial significance rests first on being called by Christ and incorporated into his apostolic mission. The supplied tradition identifies Simon as the Zealot and distinguishes Jude from Judas Iscariot; it also notes a traditional association of Jude with the Letter of Jude. Yet Scripture offers few personal biographical details, and later missionary traditions differ. The liturgy does not require uncertain details in order to honor the saints. It celebrates the sure reality that they were among those whom Jesus chose, taught, and sent.

Context: Luke places the election of the Twelve after Jesus withdraws to the mountain and spends the night in prayer to God. The choice is thus disclosed within the Son’s communion with the Father. Apostolic ministry is not an initiative devised apart from God’s will, nor is it a privilege detached from discipleship. Jesus calls from among his disciples and names twelve apostles. The number evokes the renewal of Israel: Christ gathers a people around himself and establishes a visible apostolic foundation for his mission. The list includes persons of differing names and backgrounds, including Simon called the Zealot. Their unity is not presented as the result of natural similarity. It arises from the Lord’s summons and is sustained by remaining with him. The Church continues to receive this pattern: prayer before mission, communion before division, and Christ’s call before personal distinction.

Psalm: Psalm 19 contemplates a proclamation that fills the world. The heavens declare the glory of God; day and night pour forth knowledge; their witness reaches to the ends of the earth. This is not verbal preaching in the ordinary human manner, but creation’s continual testimony to its Creator. On an apostolic feast, the psalm illumines the missionary breadth of the Gospel. The God whose glory is manifested in the ordered beauty of creation wills that the saving knowledge of Christ be made known among all peoples. The apostolic proclamation does not compete with creation’s praise; it gives voice to the Creator’s fullest saving purpose in the crucified and risen Son. The Church hears the psalm as an invitation to adoration before it speaks in mission. Those who proclaim Christ must first recognize that all creation belongs to God and already bears witness to his glory.

Gospel: The Gospel list is also marked by sobriety. Simon and Jude are not isolated from the other apostles as though holiness depended upon prominence in the narrative. They stand in the communion of the Twelve. This guards against measuring sanctity by the amount of remembered activity or recorded speech. Their witness is apostolic because it belongs to Christ’s own sending. Simon’s designation, the Zealot, distinguishes him within the list, but Luke’s central emphasis remains Jesus’ authority to appoint apostles. Jude is named as Judas son of James and thereby differentiated from Judas Iscariot. The later customary name Jude aids the Church’s remembrance, while the text itself keeps attention fixed upon the Lord who knows and calls each disciple. In this light, the feast honors hidden fidelity: a life truly known to God and made fruitful through belonging to Christ’s mission.

Saints: Ephesians provides the theological center for the feast. Paul tells Gentile Christians that they are no longer strangers and aliens, but fellow citizens with the holy ones and members of God’s household. The Church is portrayed as a building founded upon apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone. A cornerstone gives cohesion and orientation; without Christ, no apostolic foundation could stand as God’s holy dwelling. The apostles are foundational because they bear authoritative witness to Christ, receive his teaching, and serve the transmission of the Gospel. Simon and Jude are therefore honored neither as independent sources of revelation nor as distant religious heroes, but as servants of the one Lord whose Church is built into a sacred temple. The Spirit brings this construction to fulfillment by making believers a dwelling place for God.

Saints: The diversity of the Twelve is important for the Church’s understanding of unity. The supplied profile rightly observes that Jesus creates a new people whose unity comes from his call rather than identical backgrounds. Simon and Jude manifest this truth simply by their shared place among the apostles. The Church’s communion is sacramental and doctrinal: she is gathered by Christ, founded on apostolic witness, and enlivened by the Holy Spirit. Such unity cannot be reduced to agreement in temperament, preference, or human origin. It is received as grace and preserved through fidelity to the Lord. The apostles direct the Church away from any self-made religion and toward the faith handed on from Christ. Their feast thus calls believers to hear the apostolic Scriptures, confess the Church’s faith, and remain united to the cornerstone.

Today: The readings invite a prayerful and ecclesial form of Christian discipleship. Jesus’ night of prayer teaches that discernment and mission must remain before the Father. Ephesians teaches that no baptized person is merely an outsider in God’s household; all are being joined into the holy dwelling formed in Christ. Psalm 19 teaches awe before the Creator whose glory fills the earth. Saints Simon and Jude, whose individual histories are only lightly recorded in Scripture, teach perseverance without seeking notice. Their memorial asks the Church to cherish apostolic teaching, pray faithfully, witness with courage, and seek unity in the Lord. When Christians remain close to Christ the cornerstone, they do not lose their distinctness; rather, their lives are ordered toward the one communion he establishes. In that communion, the Gospel can be announced as God’s gift for the whole world.
